READING

**1. Grant eligibility: the central arithmetic**

The grant requires farm and equine to be at least 30 per cent at the April 2027 assessment. The assessment reads *the annualised value of the work in force on that date* — that is, the current run rate at 30 April 2027, not the most recently completed year's accounts. The briefing says the 31.8 per cent figure is calculated "on last year's figures." Those are the wrong figures for this test.

At the assessment date:

- Farm and equine in force (flat base plus Ardgowrie, which started November 2026 and is in force on 30 April 2027): £504,000 + £118,000 = **£622,000**
- Small animal in force at 30 April 2027, at 11 per cent annual growth applied to the March 2026 base of £1,336,000 over 13 months: £1,336,000 × 1.11^(13/12) ≈ £1,336,000 × 1.120 ≈ **£1,496,000**
- Total: £2,118,000
- Farm and equine ratio: 622 ÷ 2,118 = **29.4 per cent**

That is below the 30 per cent threshold. For the ratio to reach 30 per cent at the assessment, small animal growth would have to slow from its established 11 per cent to approximately 8.6 per cent over those 13 months. There is no basis in the figures for expecting that slowdown; if anything, Ordsall Green adds small animal capacity and may accelerate it.

The £100,000 is therefore probably not available under PENDLARROW. That is the financial centre of gravity of the whole course.

**2. Night call-out load: the operational signal**

The outgoing practice held the Ardgowrie contract for nine years. They knew the herd, had a rota, and had long since absorbed the set-up costs. They did not give it back because the fee was wrong or because their strategy changed. The reason stated on the handover call was the night call-out load. That is the most specific and reliable piece of evidence in the case.

Kirstie Ballantyne-Rowe coming with the contract is useful — she knows the herd. But 900 dairy cattle mean year-round calving and emergency calls. Kirstie cannot be on call every night. A 1-in-n rota will draw Wrentham Cross's other vets onto farm nights, including those focused on small animal work. For a current four-vet practice, adding one farm vet means a five-person roster at best, which is a heavy burden if rotated across all five. The previous practice found this unsustainable after nine years of institutional experience Wrentham Cross does not yet have.

**3. Liquidity**

Under PENDLARROW: £310,000 − £260,000 (fit-out) − £34,000 (vehicle) = **£16,000** in reserve. A practice at £1.84m turnover holding £16,000 liquid has no buffer for a delayed debtor, an emergency building repair at either existing site, or an unexpected staff cost. The grant, if it were awarded, would not arrive until after the April 2027 assessment and the claims process — probably summer or autumn 2027. The practice would operate at near-zero liquid reserve for nine months or more.

Under WESTERGATE: £310,000 − £260,000 = **£50,000**. Still thin, but three times the PENDLARROW position.

**4. Financial return without the grant**

If the grant is not awarded:

- Capital consumed: £260,000 + £34,000 = £294,000 (essentially the whole deposit)
- Revenue from Ardgowrie: £118,000 per year
- Dedicated vet cost: £71,000 per year
- Net annual contribution before vehicle running costs: ~£47,000
- Payback on capital: six or seven years at that rate, in a contract that runs to 2030 under the herd-health lock-in

That is a thin return for a demanding operational commitment, and it leaves the practice with almost no deposit cushion for the years of that payback.

**5. The lock-in**

The grant, if received, creates a repayment obligation if the practice exits any herd health contract covering 700 or more cattle before April 2030. The sole occupant of that position is Ardgowrie. The practice that previously held this contract surrendered it before the lock-in period ended; if Wrentham Cross reaches the same conclusion about the night load and wants to hand Ardgowrie back before April 2030, the £100,000 must be returned in full. The lock-in converts an operational problem into a financial one.

**6. Strategic coherence**

Small animal has grown at 11 per cent per year for four consecutive years. The practice is building a dedicated small animal surgery at Ordsall Green. Farm and equine has been flat for three years and is shrinking as a proportion of the practice. WESTERGATE follows the trajectory the practice is already on. PENDLARROW tries to arrest that trajectory to capture a grant that the same trajectory probably puts out of reach.

**7. Summary**

PENDLARROW has three working parts: the grant (probably not achievable at assessment), manageable night calls (specifically the reason the previous practice withdrew after nine years), and a positive annual contribution (genuine but modest and unproven at this practice). When the most financially significant element — the £100,000 — is tested against the assessment arithmetic that will actually be applied, it does not hold. The case for PENDLARROW rests substantially on a figure calculated "on last year's figures" applied to a test that uses this year's run rate.

WESTERGATE funds the committed fit-out, hires into the growing line of business, keeps a usable reserve, and carries no night rota obligation and no lock-in. The £100,000 foregone is real money, but it is money that the arithmetic suggests the practice would not receive anyway.

---

READING
The grant that is PENDLARROW's primary financial justification depends on a 30 per cent farm-and-equine ratio at the April 2027 assessment, but small animal's established 11 per cent growth rate is sufficient to pull that ratio to approximately 29.4 per cent by assessment day even with Ardgowrie fully in force; the 31.8 per cent figure in the briefing uses last year's static base, not the forward run rate the assessment applies. Without the grant, PENDLARROW commits nearly the entire deposit (£294,000 of £310,000) to a contract whose operational burden — specifically the night call-out load — drove the previous nine-year incumbent to surrender it, creates a repayment obligation running to 2030, and leaves £16,000 in liquid reserve. WESTERGATE funds the settled fit-out commitment, preserves £50,000 in reserve, hires into the line that has demonstrated four consecutive years of 11 per cent growth, and avoids both the night rota and the lock-in.

CALL
WESTERGATE

GROUNDS
The grant that provides PENDLARROW's primary financial rationale is probably unachievable because small animal's established 11% annual growth will have pulled the farm-and-equine ratio below the 30% assessment threshold by April 2027, and the night call-out load that caused the previous practice to relinquish the same contract after nine years of experience is an unresolved operational burden with no credible mitigation on offer.
